claims.text: A thin, coherent tungsten interlayer between HEA layers will promote a transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
The tungsten interlayer will reduce interface diffusivity.
Coherency strains introduced by the tungsten interlayer will activate dislocation motion.
Diffusion-mediated creep is dominant at intermediate high temperatures in HEA multilayers with incoherent or partially coherent interfaces.
A nanometer-scale tungsten layer can form a coherent interface between adjacent HEA layers.
The coherent tungsten interlayer will maintain lattice alignment with the HEA layers.
Maintaining interfacial coherency with tungsten will reduce interface defects.
Maintaining interfacial coherency with tungsten will enhance mechanical continuity across HEA layers.
A coherent tungsten interface provides a higher energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
Decreasing interfacial atomic diffusion will shift the active creep mechanism toward dislocation motion.
Dislocation-mediated creep in the proposed multilayer will be accommodated through lattice glide.
At identical temperature and stress, tungsten-interlayer HEA multilayers will have a lower diffusion-linked creep strain rate than controls without tungsten.
At identical temperature and stress, tungsten-interlayer HEA multilayers will exhibit a higher dislocation density than controls without tungsten.
HEA multilayers without tungsten interlayers exhibit predominantly diffusion-mediated creep.
HEA multilayers without tungsten interlayers exhibit minimal dislocation activity at their interfaces.
The proposed transition will occur only within a temperature-and-stress window where neither diffusion creep nor dislocation-mediated creep is already overwhelmingly favored.
An excessively thick or poorly integrated tungsten layer may prevent the proposed creep-mechanism transition.
